title: "Session 7: Plotting Further — Bar Charts, Colors, Epicurves, and Facets"
subtitle: "Bar charts of counts and values, choosing colors, epidemic curves, facets, and saving plots"
---

::: downloads
[⬇ Student script](https://github.com/CWML/CWML-R-Hands-on-Workshop-Series/blob/main/student_scripts/Session%207%20-%20Plotting%20Further_STUDENT.R){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm} [⬇ Solutions](https://github.com/CWML/CWML-R-Hands-on-Workshop-Series/blob/main/solutions/Session%207%20-%20Plotting%20Further_SOLUTIONS.R){.btn .btn-outline-secondary .btn-sm} [⬇ Whole workshop folder (ZIP)](https://github.com/CWML/CWML-R-Hands-on-Workshop-Series/archive/refs/heads/main.zip){.btn .btn-outline-secondary .btn-sm}
:::

::: callout-note
## In this session you will learn to

1.  Make bar charts of counts (`geom_bar()`) and of values you calculated (`geom_col()`)
2.  Order bars sensibly and choose stacked, side-by-side, or 100% bars
3.  Choose colors on purpose with `scale_fill_manual()`
4.  Make an epidemic curve from dates
5.  Split a plot into small multiples with `facet_wrap()`
6.  Save plots to files with `ggsave()`

**Before you start:** open the workshop folder in Positron (**File → Open Folder...**) and open `student_scripts/Session 7 - Plotting Further_STUDENT.R`. This session starts from `processed_data/combined_linelist.rds` and `processed_data/measles_final.rds`, the files you made in Session 3. Missed a session? Ready-made copies are already in `processed_data/`.
:::

# Part 1: Set up

Load the packages, import the finished linelist, and put the categories in a sensible order (the same as Session 6):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(rio)

linelist <- import(here("processed_data", "combined_linelist.rds"), trust = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    age_cat = fct_relevel(age_cat, "Under 18", "18-29", "30-39", "40-49",
                          "50-59", "60-69", "70-79", "80+", "Unknown"),
    outcome = fct_relevel(outcome, "Recover", "Death", "Unknown")
  )
```
:::


::: callout-tip
## Save your colors once

Saving your colors in a **named vector** means every plot uses the **same color for the same category**:

`vacc_colors <- c("Yes" = "#2a78d6", "No" = "#eb6834", "Unknown" = "#9a9a95")`

You will use these colors in Part 4.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT (3 min): set up the measles data

Import `measles_final.rds` as `measles`, `fct_relevel()` `age_cat` and `vaccinated` (same as Session 6), and save `vacc_colors` (above).

✅ **Check:** `vacc_colors` prints three named colors

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
measles <- import(here("processed_data", "measles_final.rds"), trust = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    age_cat    = fct_relevel(age_cat, "Under 5", "5-9", "10-14", "15+", "Unknown"),
    vaccinated = fct_relevel(vaccinated, "Yes", "No", "Unknown")
  )

vacc_colors <- c("Yes" = "#2a78d6", "No" = "#eb6834", "Unknown" = "#9a9a95")
vacc_colors
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
      Yes        No   Unknown 
"#2a78d6" "#eb6834" "#9a9a95" 
```


:::
:::


The same import pipeline as Session 6, plus a named color vector: each name (`"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unknown"`) is a category, and each value is its color.
:::
:::

# Part 2: Bar charts of counts: `geom_bar()`

`geom_bar()` **counts the rows** in each category for you — you only give it `x`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = hospital_name)) +
  geom_bar()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-plotting-further_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-alt='Vertical bar chart of cases by hospital in gray. The hospital names on the x-axis overlap and are hard to read. Other/Unknown has the most cases (about 2,350), then Regional Medical center (about 1,800).' width=672}
:::
:::


The labels overlap. Put the categories on the **y-axis** instead to get horizontal bars:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(y = hospital_name)) +
  geom_bar()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-plotting-further_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-alt='Horizontal bar chart of cases by hospital in gray. The hospital names on the y-axis are now easy to read, but the bars are in alphabetical order.' width=672}
:::
:::


## Order the bars

Alphabetical order rarely helps. `fct_infreq()` orders by count (most common first), and `fct_rev()` flips it so the longest bar is at the top:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(y = fct_rev(fct_infreq(hospital_name)))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#2a78d6") +
  labs(title = "Cases by hospital", x = "Number of cases", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-plotting-further_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-alt='Horizontal bar chart titled Cases by hospital in blue, sorted from most to fewest cases: Other/Unknown, Regional Medical center, Military Hospital, Central Hospital, St. Mark\'s Maternity Hospital, HMO Health, and Premiere Health.' width=672}
:::
:::


`y = NULL` removes an axis title the reader doesn't need.

## Fill by a second variable

Map `fill` to split each bar. The `position` argument controls how the pieces are arranged:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# "stack" (the default): counts, stacked
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_cat, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "stack")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-plotting-further_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-alt='Stacked bar chart of case counts by age group, split by outcome. The Under 18 group is by far the largest (about 4,000 cases), so outcomes in the older groups are hard to compare.' width=672}
:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# "fill": every bar is 100% — compares PROPORTIONS across groups
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_cat, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-plotting-further_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-alt='100% stacked bar chart of outcome by age group: each bar is split into Recover, Death, and Unknown and reaches the same height, so proportions can be compared. The small older groups vary the most.' width=672}
:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# "dodge": side by side — compares COUNTS within each group
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_cat, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-plotting-further_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){fig-alt='Bar chart with side-by-side bars for Recover, Death, and Unknown in each age group. Under 18 has the tallest bars, and deaths outnumber recoveries in most age groups.' width=672}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🤔 Think about it: which version answers "do older patients die more often?"

The 100% `"fill"` version. The stacked version mostly shows that there are many more young patients than old ones, so the small bars for older groups are hard to compare.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT (3 min): cases by district

Make a horizontal bar chart of measles cases by district, longest bar on top.

✅ **Check:** North is at the top; Unknown is at the bottom

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = measles, mapping = aes(y = fct_rev(fct_infreq(district)))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#2a78d6") +
  labs(title = "Measles cases by district", x = "Number of cases", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-plotting-further_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-alt='Horizontal bar chart of measles cases by district in blue, longest at the top: North (342), South (284), East (223), West (170), Central (110), and Unknown (34).' width=672}
:::
:::


`fct_infreq()` puts North (342 cases) first, and `fct_rev()` moves it to the top. Unknown (34 cases) ends up at the bottom.
:::
:::

# Part 3: Bar charts of values: `geom_col()`

When **you** have already calculated the numbers (with `count()` or `summarise()` from Session 5), use `geom_col()` and give it both `x` and `y`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
death_by_age <- linelist %>%
  filter(outcome != "Unknown", age_cat != "Unknown") %>%
  group_by(age_cat) %>%
  summarise(
    n         = n(),
    pct_death = mean(outcome == "Death") * 100
  )

death_by_age
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 8 × 3
  age_cat      n pct_death
  <fct>    <int>     <dbl>
1 Under 18  3077      57.0
2 18-29     1146      56.5
3 30-39      435      58.9
4 40-49      190      55.3
5 50-59       53      54.7
6 60-69       24      33.3
7 70-79        6      50  
8 80+          1       0  
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = death_by_age, mapping = aes(x = age_cat, y = pct_death)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2a78d6") +
  labs(title = "Case fatality by age group", x = "Age group", y = "Deaths (% of cases)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-plotting-further_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-alt='Bar chart of the percentage of cases who died in each age group: 55 to 59% for every group under 60, 33% for 60 to 69, 50% for 70 to 79 (only 6 patients), and 0% for 80 and over (1 patient).' width=672}
:::
:::


::: callout-note
## `geom_bar()` or `geom_col()`?

`geom_bar()` counts rows for you (one row per patient): give it `x` only. `geom_col()` draws numbers you already have (one row per bar): give it `x` **and** `y`.

`fct_reorder(CATEGORY, NUMBER)` sorts the bars by the number.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🤔 Think about it: how much should we trust the 70–79 and 80+ bars?

Not much. Check `n` in `death_by_age`: the 70–79 bar is based on 6 patients and the 80+ bar on just 1. One more death or recovery would change those percentages a lot. Always look at how many cases are behind a percentage.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT (5 min): case rates by district

a)  Calculate cases per 10,000 people by district (Session 5), leaving out "Unknown".
b)  Plot it with `geom_col()`, using `x = fct_reorder(district, rate_per_10k)`.

✅ **Check:** bars from Central (lowest, 5.2) to East (highest, 22.8)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# a)
district_rates <- measles %>%
  filter(district != "Unknown") %>%
  count(district, population) %>%
  mutate(rate_per_10k = round(n / population * 10000, 1))

district_rates
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  district population   n rate_per_10k
1  Central     210000 110          5.2
2     East      98000 223         22.8
3    North     185000 342         18.5
4    South     142000 284         20.0
5     West      76500 170         22.2
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# b)
ggplot(data = district_rates, mapping = aes(x = fct_reorder(district, rate_per_10k), y = rate_per_10k)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2a78d6") +
  labs(
    title = "Measles cases per 10,000 people by district",
    x     = "District",
    y     = "Cases per 10,000 people"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-plotting-further_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-alt='Bar chart of measles cases per 10,000 people by district, sorted from lowest to highest: Central 5.2, North 18.5, South 20.0, West 22.2, and East 22.8.' width=672}
:::
:::


`count()` makes one row per district, so `geom_col()` is the right choice. North has the most cases, but Central has the largest population, so the **rates** tell a different story: East (22.8) and West (22.2) are highest, Central (5.2) is lowest.
:::
:::

# Part 4: Choosing colors

ggplot's default colors are fine for exploring, but for a report choose colors **on purpose**:

-   Use colors that people with color-vision deficiency can tell apart. **Avoid red vs green** (the most common problem pair) and two shades of the same color. Blue (`#2a78d6`) and orange (`#eb6834`) are a safe pair
-   Give "Unknown" or "Other" a **gray** (`#9a9a95`), so it doesn't compete with the real categories
-   Keep the **same color for the same category** in every plot of a report

`scale_fill_manual()` (for `fill`) and `scale_color_manual()` (for `color`) set the colors by name:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
outcome_colors <- c("Recover" = "#2a78d6", "Death" = "#eb6834", "Unknown" = "#9a9a95")

ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = age_cat, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill", color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = outcome_colors) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Outcome by age group",
    x     = "Age group",
    y     = "Percent of cases",
    fill  = "Outcome"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-plotting-further_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-alt='100% stacked bar chart of outcome by age group with chosen colors: blue for Recover, orange for Death, and gray for Unknown, with a percent y-axis and a minimal theme.' width=672}
:::
:::


-   Saving the colors as `outcome_colors` lets you reuse them in every plot
-   `color = "white"` draws a thin white line between the segments
-   `scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent)` shows 0.25 as 25%

::: callout-tip
## Need more colors?

The **viridis** scales are built into ggplot2 and are colorblind-friendly: try `scale_fill_viridis_d()` for categories.
:::

## Rotate long labels

If you keep labels on the x-axis, rotate them so they don't overlap:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = hospital_name)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#2a78d6") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-plotting-further_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){fig-alt='Vertical bar chart of cases by hospital in blue, with the hospital names rotated 45 degrees so they no longer overlap.' width=672}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT (4 min): vaccination by age group

Make a 100% bar chart of `vaccinated` by `age_cat`, with `vacc_colors`, a percent y-axis, labels, and `theme_minimal()`.

✅ **Check:** every bar reaches 100%; "Yes" is blue in every bar

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = measles, mapping = aes(x = age_cat, fill = vaccinated)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill", color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = vacc_colors) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Vaccination status of measles cases by age group",
    x     = "Age group",
    y     = "Percent of cases",
    fill  = "Vaccinated"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-plotting-further_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-alt='100% stacked bar chart of measles vaccination status by age group. In every age group most cases were unvaccinated (orange), and about a quarter were vaccinated (blue); gray shows unknown status.' width=672}
:::
:::


`position = "fill"` makes every bar 100%, and because `vacc_colors` is a **named** vector, "Yes" is always blue, "No" orange, and "Unknown" gray.
:::
:::

# Part 5: Epidemic curves

An **epidemic curve** (epicurve) shows the number of new cases over time — the most important plot in outbreak investigation. It is a histogram of a **date** column:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data = linelist, mapping = aes(x = onset_date)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 7, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-plotting-further_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){fig-alt='Weekly epidemic curve of all onset dates: a small cluster in late 2012 and early 2013, a gap, then the main outbreak from mid-2014 that peaks at about 300 cases per week in September 2014.' width=672}
:::
:::


`binwidth = 7` makes each bar one week.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🤔 Think about it: what is going on before 2014?

538 onset dates fall in 2012–2013, long before the outbreak — and every one of them belongs to a case ID that appears more than once (the duplicate IDs from Session 3), usually with the same day and month but a different year. They are almost certainly data-entry errors in the year. **Plots reveal problems tables hide:** look at the whole range first!
:::

Zoom in on the outbreak and format the date axis:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist %>%
  filter(onset_date >= as.Date("2014-01-01")) %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = onset_date)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 7, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 months", date_labels = "%b\n%Y") +
  labs(
    title    = "Epidemic curve: weekly cases by date of symptom onset",
    subtitle = "Onset dates from 2014 onward",
    x        = "Week of onset",
    y        = "Number of cases"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-plotting-further_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-alt='Epidemic curve of weekly cases from 2014 onward. Cases rise from May 2014 to a peak of about 300 per week in September 2014, then decline slowly through April 2015.' width=672}
:::
:::


-   `date_breaks = "2 months"` puts a label every two months
-   `date_labels = "%b\n%Y"` shows the short month name, a line break, and the year (`%d` = day, `%B` = full month name)

## Epicurve by outcome


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist %>%
  filter(onset_date >= as.Date("2014-01-01")) %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = onset_date, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 7, color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = outcome_colors) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 months", date_labels = "%b\n%Y") +
  labs(x = "Week of onset", y = "Number of cases", fill = "Outcome") +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-plotting-further_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){fig-alt='Epidemic curve of weekly cases from 2014 onward with each bar split by outcome: blue for Recover, orange for Death, gray for Unknown. All three outcomes rise and fall with the outbreak.' width=672}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT (5 min): the measles epicurve

Make a weekly epicurve of measles `report_date`, filled by `vaccinated`, with `vacc_colors` and `scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b")`. Save it as `measles_epicurve` — you will need it in Part 7. **Hint:** `filter(!is.na(report_date))` first. When did the outbreak peak?

✅ **Check:** the peak is in the second half of March (about 115 cases in one week)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
measles_epicurve <- measles %>%
  filter(!is.na(report_date)) %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = report_date, fill = vaccinated)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 7, color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = vacc_colors) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b") +
  labs(
    title = "Measles cases by week of report, 2024",
    x     = "Week of report",
    y     = "Number of cases",
    fill  = "Vaccinated"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

measles_epicurve
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-plotting-further_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){fig-alt='Weekly epidemic curve of measles cases in 2024 by week of report, split by vaccination status. Cases rise from February, peak in the second half of March at about 115 cases in one week, and fall through June. Most cases each week were unvaccinated (orange).' width=672}
:::
:::


The outbreak peaked in the second half of March 2024, with 117 cases in the peak week. Saving the plot as an object means it only appears when you print it (the last line).
:::
:::

# Part 6: Facets

`facet_wrap()` splits one plot into **small multiples** — one panel per category, all with the same axes so they are easy to compare:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist %>%
  filter(onset_date >= as.Date("2014-01-01"), hospital_name != "Other/Unknown") %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = onset_date)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 7, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ hospital_name) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "4 months", date_labels = "%b\n%Y") +
  labs(title = "Weekly cases by hospital", x = "Week of onset", y = "Number of cases") +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-plotting-further_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){fig-alt='Four small epidemic curves on the same axes, one per hospital: Central Hospital, Military Hospital, Regional Medical center, and St. Mark\'s Maternity Hospital. Regional Medical center has the largest outbreak, peaking at about 90 cases per week in September 2014.' width=672}
:::
:::


Facets work with any plot:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist %>%
  filter(gender != "Unknown") %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = age_years)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ gender) +
  labs(title = "Age distribution by gender", x = "Age (years)", y = "Number of cases") +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-plotting-further_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){fig-alt='Two age histograms side by side, for female and male patients. Female patients are mostly under 25, while male ages are spread more widely, up to about 75.' width=672}
:::
:::


::: callout-note
-   `facet_wrap(~ hospital_name, ncol = 2)` sets the number of columns
-   `facet_wrap(~ hospital_name, scales = "free_y")` lets each panel have its own y-axis (careful: it makes panels harder to compare)
-   `facet_grid(gender ~ outcome)` makes a grid with one variable for rows and one for columns
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT (4 min): facets

Facet your measles epicurve by district (leave out "Unknown"). Did every district peak at the same time?

✅ **Check:** five panels; every district peaks in March

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
measles %>%
  filter(!is.na(report_date), district != "Unknown") %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = report_date, fill = vaccinated)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 7, color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ district) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = vacc_colors) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 months", date_labels = "%b") +
  labs(
    title = "Measles cases by week of report and district, 2024",
    x     = "Week of report",
    y     = "Number of cases",
    fill  = "Vaccinated"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](07-plotting-further_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){fig-alt='Five small weekly epidemic curves of measles cases, one per district, with bars colored by vaccination status. Every district peaks in March 2024, and North has the most cases.' width=672}
:::
:::


Roughly, yes: every district peaks in March, at about the same time as the overall outbreak. North has the most cases (its busiest week has 39).
:::
:::

# Part 7: Saving plots

`ggsave()` saves the **last plot you made**, or a plot object you name. Save the plot as an object first:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
epicurve <- linelist %>%
  filter(onset_date >= as.Date("2014-01-01")) %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = onset_date)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 7, fill = "#2a78d6", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Weekly cases", x = "Week of onset", y = "Number of cases") +
  theme_minimal()
```
:::


Then save it to the `outputs/` folder:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggsave(here("outputs", "epicurve.png"), plot = epicurve,
       width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
```
:::


-   The file type comes from the extension: `.png` for slides and documents, `.pdf` for print
-   `width` and `height` are in inches; `dpi = 300` is print quality
-   Save plots in their own folder (here, `outputs/`) so they don't get mixed up with data

# Extra: box plots with summary labels (optional)

This optional, advanced example calculates the median and quartiles for each group with `summarise()`, turns them into text, and adds them to the plot with `geom_text()` — combining Sessions 4, 5, and 6.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# 1. Summary statistics for each gender and outcome
box_stats <- linelist %>%
  filter(gender != "Unknown", outcome != "Unknown") %>%
  group_by(gender, outcome) %>%
  summarise(
    median = median(age_years, na.rm = TRUE),
    q1     = quantile(age_years, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    q3     = quantile(age_years, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(label = paste0("Median: ", round(median, 1), "\n",
                        "Q1: ", round(q1, 1), "\n",
                        "Q3: ", round(q3, 1)))

# 2. The plot, with the labels placed beside each box
linelist %>%
  filter(gender != "Unknown", outcome != "Unknown") %>%
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = gender, y = age_years)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#2a78d6", alpha = 0.3, width = 0.35) +
  geom_text(
    data = box_stats,
    mapping = aes(x = gender, y = q3, label = label),
    nudge_x = 0.22, hjust = 0, vjust = 0, size = 2.8, color = "gray30"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ outcome) +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.4, 0.9))) +   # room on the right for the labels
  labs(
    title    = "Age distribution by gender and outcome",
    subtitle = "Labels show the median and quartiles",
    x        = "Gender",
    y        = "Age (years)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Key points

-   `geom_bar()` **counts rows** for you; `geom_col()` draws numbers you **already calculated**.
-   Order bars with `fct_infreq()` / `fct_reorder()`, and use horizontal bars (`aes(y = ...)`) for long labels.
-   `position = "stack"`, `"fill"` (100%, compares proportions), or `"dodge"` (side by side, compares counts).
-   Choose colors on purpose: colorblind-safe pairs (not red vs green), gray for "Unknown", and a named color vector with `scale_fill_manual()` so each category keeps its color.
-   An **epicurve** is a weekly histogram of a date column; format the axis with `scale_x_date()`. Look at the whole date range first — plots reveal data errors.
-   `facet_wrap(~ COLUMN)` makes small multiples with shared axes.
-   Save a plot as an object, then `ggsave(here("outputs", "file.png"), plot = ..., width, height, dpi)`.
